title: This Italian Architect Wants to Build Farms in Downtown Shanghai | 100 People With Ideas
excerpt: A metro exit, an elementary school playground, the outer wall of an old neighborhood. Fantasy, or a project that could actually work?
body:
A metro exit, an elementary school playground, the outer wall of an old neighborhood. Fantasy, or a project that could actually work?

In the second half of 2016, Shanghai's Jiangsu Road metro station may look a little different. A patch of green will appear on the plaza outside it: a small farm with fish in it, growing fruit, vegetables and medicinal herbs. Similar farms are planned for the playground of an elementary school on Yuyuan Road and inside an old shikumen neighborhood on Jiangsu Road.

All of them belong to a project called Edible City. The name may be unfamiliar, but the idea is the one Europe and the US now call urban agriculture. Its advocates say it does two things at once: it makes a neighborhood better to live in, and it turns idle space into somewhere people actually go.

The project is led by the Italian firm DEDO Design, and it now has the backing of the Changning district government.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702124136Qemy2jJ65BaEsHMO.jpg-w600)

![Edible City (rendering)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702124137c93UrJsmojNvpbLB.jpg-w600)

DEDO Design was founded in Shanghai by the Italian designer Nong Qing (her real name is Nunzia Carbone). Its clients so far include the French government, the government of China's Anhui province, Maserati, Ferrari, General Electric and Fujitsu. The work runs from large-scale urban planning and architecture to a good number of old-building renovations and interiors. Edible City is not a typical DEDO project.

But the designers wanted to change something about Shanghai, the city they live in every day.

"Shanghai does its greenery well, but from the point of view of food production and urban farming, it isn't enough," Nong Qing said. "There are a lot of parks here, but every one of them is cut off from the others. What we will eventually do is link the parks with green corridors, into a green network." What strings those corridors and that network together are the small farms she is building now — the Edible Station and the Edible School.

She believes this can build a new relationship between residents and nature, and reshape the city's space and daily life. "Think of the people who commute by metro. They walk out of the station into a gentle, pretty place, like the countryside. How good would that feel?"

Nong Qing first came to Shanghai in 2001, to design a building for an English-language school for an Italian client. Before that she had worked at architecture firms in London, Paris and New York. After the language-school job she decided to settle in China and start her own company.

Every friend of hers found the decision baffling — Shanghai then was very different from Shanghai now, less open, more traditional in its view of design. But Nong Qing thought architects here had more choice and more freedom. To her it looked like an opening.

The early research for Edible City came back fairly positive too. DEDO worked with Tongji University and NYU Shanghai on surveys of what people wanted. The Shanghai residents they interviewed kept returning to food quality and food safety. "People don't know how their food is produced, or what technology went into it, so food safety is what worries them most. And of course they very much want a good relationship with nature," Nong Qing said.

The research produced these numbers: by 2035, 70% of China's population will live in cities; 95% of Chinese people care about farming methods, how much pesticide and fertilizer is used, and how food is processed afterwards; and 60% of Shanghai residents would give up part of their own living space to grow food on it.

Those results convinced DEDO to go ahead. The firm started the project two years ago, which now makes it one of the faster movers in this field in China.

Europe, the US and Asian countries like Japan and South Korea have had comparable projects for a while. QDaily has reported on ["Farm-X," designed by the Zurich firm Conceptual Devices](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/10495.html), which turned 1,000 square meters of abandoned factory and warehouse land into a farm; it uses a particular hydroponic growing technique and round-the-clock climate monitoring, and can produce up to 5 tons of fresh food a day. In Paris, [the rooftop of the flagship store of the department store chain Galeries Lafayette was also converted into a farm](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/10992.html), with a soilless growing system that uses wool and hemp as its medium and recycles the water through the irrigation system.

DEDO's approach is more varied. It has finished designs for three pilot sites in Changning. The Edible Station is a strip of green on the plaza outside a metro station, aimed at hurried commuters. The Edible School sits on the playground of an elementary school on Yuyuan Road, where children can climb into a treehouse to grow fruit, vegetables and other crops. Both include planting beds and a fish pond. The designers chose an aquaponic system that puts fish farming and hydroponic plants together: the fish feed the plants, and the water is then cleaned, filtered and used again.

The third pilot, the Edible Community, is set in an old lilong in Changning, and is the only vertical one of the three. The designers want to cover the outer walls of the lilong houses with soil, plants and vegetables, making green space that is built into the building.

The first two will be finished in 2016. After that, green farms around Shanghai will supply materials and technical support, and a property management company will be hired to run them. The firm is drawing up construction documents and budgets, showing the project to communities and schools that might take part, and looking for sponsors to fund it.

![From top to bottom: the Edible Station, the Edible School, the Edible Community (renderings)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702124137AqXvoSltFJgPiUdb.jpg-w600)

Taken as a whole, Edible City is closer to an experiment. Much of it is still unsettled: how food would be supplied, what the daily upkeep involves, how food safety would be guaranteed.

Dong Xuelian, an architect and associate at DEDO Design, says the team has always been interested in new technology and green architecture, and that this is a large part of why it wins governments and other big clients.

Beyond the company website there isn't much information about DEDO, and Nong Qing rarely gives interviews. But she appears in public more than she used to, taking the project to the 2015 Shanghai International Urban Planning and Architecture Expo and the 2016 Shanghai "Design Transformation" art and design exhibition.

Years of dealing with clients may help her sell this one.

DEDO once designed a sunken plaza, for instance, and the client felt that walking downward carried a bad meaning by local custom. The architects had to redo the entrance: first a flight of steps going up, then back down again.

Sometimes they have to settle a conflict between a building's presence and its respect for the natural setting. Take a museum now underway in Anhui. The client is a development zone government, which wants a museum, an art gallery and a concert hall combined into one building beside a lake, and wants it to be a landmark with impact.

To keep the building from standing too tall and too abrupt against the landscape, DEDO's architects decided to spread it sideways instead. It covers more ground, and the plan of the landscape is woven into the plan of the building; the water and greenery worked into it become the atrium planting, the courtyards and the small garden structures.

![A museum in Anhui (rendering)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702124138KcFAmqHIWr1hxOwn.jpg-w600)

"With Chinese clients, holding on to our own style really does take more effort in the talking," Dong Xuelian said. Chinese clients tend to have a lot of "random ideas."

Edible City, though, is no longer a client's project. The firm's designers, who come from several countries, are getting closer than before to how local people behave. Ahead of them is a process in which every last detail has to be asked about.

They go looking for unused space all over the city, and have to meet a great many people, the elderly and children included: showing the project to everyone involved, surveying, asking, talking; watching how Chinese clients live at close range, getting a feel for what they think and need. Which is why Nong Qing expects the project to be "a challenge, but unusually interesting."

Fifteen years in China have made urban life here ordinary to her. She lives in an old house downtown and knows Shanghai's lanes well. Except when it is windy or raining, she walks 40 minutes to work every day, taking the small streets on purpose. She still likes watching the people passing and the residents along the way, because "you often find all kinds of surprising, interesting grassroots invention."

She and DEDO's architects want to understand this city better. Doing projects is one way to learn it.

In practical terms, if Edible City is proved workable, it can be applied to other urban planning and architecture projects later; the "urban farm" can be exported as a complete, tested package of techniques, and DEDO itself can move into consulting and management. All of which assumes everything goes smoothly.
